title: node-telemetry-semantic-index-and-routing-guidelines
content:
Purpose
---
Notes and a proposed design for a lightweight, semantic node index used by the control plane and routing layer. Focus: normalize node descriptors (labels, GPU fingerprints, host metadata), derive a compact health score, and make routing decisions in multi-region deployments. This is an operational-first draft: tradeoffs favor predictable behavior and easy rollout.

Background / problem summary
---
We currently have multiple partial inventories: kube node labels, fleet registry entries, raw telemetry streams (Prometheus + hostbeat), and ad-hoc GPU probing results. Routing and placement logic ends up querying several services or using heuristics embedded in callers. This causes inconsistent routing decisions across hosted, dedicated, and private installs and makes rollout of new routing rules high-friction.

Goals
---
- Provide a single, compact node descriptor that is: machine-readable, versioned, and cheap to evaluate at request time.
- Normalize GPU capability reporting (model family, memory, GPU compute class, fp16/ampere/inferece-optimized flags).
- Generate a deterministic health score from telemetry signals that is transparent and debuggable.
- Support multi-region routing policies with clear fallback tiers and cost/tier awareness.
- Keep control plane scaling-friendly: incremental deltas, local caches with TTL, and bounded descriptor size.

High-level design
---
1) Semantic node index (SNI)
   - Each node publishes a single SNI descriptor (small JSON blob, <2KB typical) to the registry. The registry stores the latest descriptor per node id and exposes a streaming delta API and compact versioned snapshots.
   - Descriptor fields (flattened, example shown later) cover identity (node id, region, AZ), hardware (gpu_families, gpu_memory_gb, vram_util_quanta), software (driver_version, runtime_version, container_runtime), labels (application tags), and synthesized_health_score.

2) Telemetry normalization
   - Ingest sources: node-exporter/Prometheus metrics, nvidia-smi probes, agent-side heartbeat, and periodic GPU probe job run by infra.
   - Normalizer service collapses metrics into canonical metrics: gpu_temp_c, gpu_free_mem_mb, gpu_total_mem_mb, cuda_driver_mismatch (bool), pci_errors_15min, oom_kills_1h, kernel_msg_errors_1h, last_heartbeat_ts.
   - Normalizer also runs fingerprinting: map reported device name strings to normalized families (e.g., "A100-40GB" -> "a100-40", heuristic rules + manual mappings maintained in repo).

3) Health scoring heuristic (deterministic, easy to reproduce)
   - Score is integer 0..100 where 100 == perfect. Lower means less desirable for low-latency routing.
   - Base components (weights are configurable via feature flag):
       * heartbeat freshness (max staleness 60s -> 0 penalty; >60s penalize linearly up to 30s of extra = -20)
       * gpu_free_mem_pct (if <20% -> -25; 20-50% -> -10)
       * gpu_temp_c (if >85C -> -30; 75-85C -> -10)
       * pci_errors / kernel errors (any non-zero in last 15m -> -40)
       * driver/runtime mismatch (bool -> -50 if true)
       * maintenance mode label (explicit label -> -100 to exclude)
   - Final score = clamp(0, 100, 100 + sum(penalties)). All penalties are negative.
   - The node descriptor stores both the raw signals and the final score plus a brief reason list (human-readable strings) to aid debugging.

4) Routing policy primitives
   - Region affinity: prefer nodes in same region up to a soft threshold (e.g., health_score >= 65).
   - Cost-aware tiering: nodes can be tiered (on-demand, reserved, spot/burst). Routing policy will prefer reserved for throughput-critical workloads, fall back to on-demand, then spot when cost priority is highest.
   - GPU capability matching: routing checks required gpu_capabilities (fp16, tensor cores, vram_min) vs node descriptor. Exact-match for capability booleans, >= for numeric.
   - Health gates: nodes with score < 30 are excluded from latency-sensitive SLOs by default.
   - Fallback matrix example: same-region preferred -> same-region degraded (lower score) -> cross-region reserved -> cross-region on-demand -> cached response / degraded model variant.

5) Control plane: registry, delta stream, local cache model
   - Registry: authoritative store of node descriptors. Provides restful snapshot endpoints and a gRPC streaming delta. Snapshots are gzipped and periodically produced; deltas are small protobufs that reference node_id + updated fields.
   - Local caches: each routing decision service keeps an in-memory cache of relevant nodes (per-region subset). Cache invalidation via delta stream; re-fetch on missed deltas or staleness TTL (e.g., 90s).
   - Consistency model: eventual with last-writer-wins per node_id + change_ts. Accept small windows of staleness for routing decisions; use health_score as primary guard.

6) Size and privacy considerations
   - Keep descriptor small: flatten arrays to lists of short tokens, avoid verbose labels. Redact user-sensitive metadata (customer tags) in hosted mode; private deployments can opt-in to additional fields.

Descriptor example (illustrative snippet; stored as a single-line compact JSON in registry)
{
  "node_id": "node-az3-23112",
  "region": "us-west-2",
  "az": "az3",
  "gpu_families": ["a100-40"],
  "gpu_total_mem_mb": 40536,
  "gpu_free_mem_mb": 29812,
  "driver_version": "535.86.10",
  "runtime_version": "triton-2.5",
  "labels": ["dedicated:inference", "env:prod"],
  "health_score": "78",
  "health_reasons": ["minor_memory_pressure", "heartbeat_12s"]
}

Operational playbook / rollout steps
---
- Stage 1 (pilot): enable SNI write-only. Normalizer produces descriptors, registry accepts them, but routing still uses existing heuristics. Run pilot on a single region and <5% traffic routed via new policy.
- Stage 2 (observe): enable read from registry in non-critical path (canary routes). Compare decisions and produce delta reports for mismatches.
- Stage 3 (soft switch): enable new routing primitives with weight-based blending (10% -> 50% -> 100%). Monitor model QoE, tail latency and cost.
- Stage 4 (hard switch): deprecate legacy heuristics and adopt SNI registry as single source-of-truth.

Open questions / tradeoffs
---
- Do we want a global unique node id or regional-prefixed id? Prefer global to avoid collisions but ensure compactness.
- How to handle private deployments where telemetry flows are restricted? Option: local-only registry with optional upstream reporting.
- Weight tuning: we need a small experiments framework (eval traffic) to tune score weights.
- Security: signed descriptors to prevent accidental spoofing in hybrid-peering scenarios.

Notes to reviewers
---
This doc intentionally biases toward operational simplicity. If you want more complex consistency (e.g., CRDT-based merges) or stronger guarantees on descriptor freshness, call it out and provide a concrete reason. The goal for the first iteration is: predictable, explainable routing decisions and a single place operators can look when something routes wrongly.
